extracted.intended_audience: postsecondary mathematics instructors, graduate teaching assistants, and mathematics education practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for structuring classroom tasks, participation, and norms to support authentic mathematical practice, equitable participation, and productive struggle in college-level mathematics courses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Task framing (open versus closed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose how open or closed to make a task: e.g., asking “Which numbers can you express with four fours? Can you express all numbers?” (open) versus “Find expressions for all numbers from 0 to 100 using combinations of four fours.” (closed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A more closed framing lessens cognitive demand because students do less of the mathematical thinking; use closed framings intentionally (for example, when you want students to practice a particular procedural skill). When choosing tasks, also consider how you will enact them so students get to do the meaningful thinking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enact tasks to ensure student sense-making
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting a task is not sufficient — you must enact it in a way that ensures students engage in the intended mathematical thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think about the prompts, supports, and constraints you give so students are pushed to do meaningful thinking rather than just follow procedures or reproduce known answers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray mathematics authentically (front vs back door)
rubrics_metrics.description: Portray mathematics as the messy, informal, exploratory work that mathematicians actually do (the 'back' of mathematics), not only the neatly packaged theorems and proofs students usually see (the 'front').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model struggle, false starts, conjecturing, drawing pictures, and informal thinking. Let students see you get stuck and get unstuck to normalize the inquiry process and the messiness required to produce polished mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote mathematical practices / habits of mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide opportunities for students to engage in authentic practices such as making conjectures, exploring open-ended problems, proving and argumentation, modeling, and generalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid teaching in a purely procedural way that focuses on covering content; instead design activities that permit the development of these practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalize failure and productive struggle
rubrics_metrics.description: Create an atmosphere where exploration, mistakes, false starts, and in-progress ideas are expected and valued as part of learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use strategies like 'my favorite no' (selecting and discussing an interesting incorrect student solution) and 'failure portfolios' (students collect mistakes and reflect on overcoming them). Frame challenges as natural and necessary; use the zone of proximal development to push students just beyond current capabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use social engagement and feedback as learning mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Leverage peer explanation, feedback, and community participation because students deepen understanding through sharing in-progress ideas — correctness is not required for learning to occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide many opportunities for students to practice and receive feedback from instructors and peers; emphasize process over immediate correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop and use Mathematical Knowledge for Teaching (MKT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructors should acquire knowledge not only of content but of how students typically think about that content, common conceptual challenges, and students' resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This knowledge supports designing activities and eliciting student thinking; curricular materials that include common student thinking/sample work can accelerate development. Build MKT by making student thinking a focus (see Chapters 5 and 6 references).

rubrics_metrics.name: Humanize the instructor and the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Model yourself as a mathematician on a learning journey and humanize mathematics through history and real-world connections so students see mathematics as a human endeavor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Share appropriate personal struggles, historical context, and connections to societal issues; discuss why concepts (e.g., limits) developed historically and highlight the humans involved, including messy or political aspects of historiography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide diverse role models and representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Intentionally bring role models that reflect students' identities (e.g., invite members of campus programs, share biographies of diverse mathematicians, use communities that highlight contributions from different groups).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use guest visits, readings (e.g., Living Proof, Testimonios), social media, and curated communities (Mathematically Gifted & Black, Lathisms, Indigenous Mathematicians, Spectra, Sines of Disability) to disrupt narrow stereotypes about who can be a mathematician.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface and deconstruct stereotypes about mathematicians
rubrics_metrics.description: Actively surface students' stereotypes and implicit biases (about who does mathematics and what mathematicians look/act like) and discuss why they are false or problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tasks like 'draw a mathematician' and guided discussion prompts (What did you draw? Why? Do you agree with that stereotype? Why do those stereotypes exist? What would it take to change them?) to provoke reflection and dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make student thinking a central focus and collect participation data
rubrics_metrics.description: Elicit, analyze, and build on student thinking consistently; gather data about participation patterns (including by social markers) to guide equitable instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use targeted strategies with social-marker specificity to identify students perceived as low status, identify their mathematical contributions, and make those contributions public (three-step process). More data about participation enables disrupting classroom hierarchies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose participation structures aligned to learning goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Select from individual, partner, group, or whole-class formats because different formats support different learning goals and provide different opportunities for students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why a given structure is useful for the activity; if you choose partner or group formats, give clear directions and supports to ensure participation and safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide clear directions and explicit framing for participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Always give explicit, concrete instructions for how to participate (who to work with, what to do, time limits), rather than vague invites like 'you can talk to a peer if you'd like.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use physical cues and scripting (e.g., 'turn your desk to the person next to you and have a conversation for one minute'). If students don't follow directions, check in individually and ask 'What would make this learning opportunity more accessible to you?' Avoid leaving participation to chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use individual think time and pausing strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate intentional pauses for individual processing (e.g., 'I'm going to pause for a minute so you can process...') and routines like think-pair-share to improve response quality and equity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research shows pauses increase both proportion of questions students can answer and the depth of responses; individual work is useful for building procedural fluency and for preparing students to engage in peer discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design partner work with explicit norms and turn-taking
rubrics_metrics.description: When using partner work, provide structures (e.g., timed turns: 'first partner talks for a minute, then the other responds') to prevent domination and to ensure both students speak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partner work is flexible, supports tutoring effects, is good for moderate-complexity problem solving and structured peer feedback, and serves as a pre-check before whole-class discussion so every student has something to contribute. Monitor for subtle inequities in talk by race/gender.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overreliance on lecture and disconnected procedural practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use class time primarily for fast-paced lectures that leave no processing time nor for disconnected procedural drills that do not leverage social learning benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve procedural practice for independent work or short in-class diagnostics; use class time to engage social aspects of learning and conceptual sense-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be intentional and data-driven to support marginalized students
rubrics_metrics.description: Use social-marker-specific intentionality when applying strategies so they actually improve equity rather than being neutral or reproducing hierarchies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gather local data about participation patterns and use it to identify low-status students, target elicitation strategies toward minoritized students, and publicly position their contributions as competent to reverse historical inequities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use formative assessment artifacts (e.g., failure portfolios) to promote reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: Have students collect and reflect on mistakes and partial attempts (failure portfolios) and use quick formative checks (e.g., index card sorting for 'my favorite no') to surface learning opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These artifacts honor partial attempts, prompt reflection on overcoming errors, and provide material for whole-class discussion that focuses on what was done well and where mistakes occurred.
